analysis.title: The AI disconnect: the AI crash has a problem, earnings aren't crashing
key_insights: The Market Ear summarizes a JPM bullish Asian tech roadmap published just before the latest selloff. JPM's central argument was that valuations already priced in an earnings downturn that was not showing up in the data. Selling has intensified since.

Asian tech had suffered its fourth 20%+ correction since 2022 when JPM published. Roughly 80% of companies still had positive earnings revisions, and valuations had compressed toward historical averages.
Per JPM, forward P/E for Asian tech excluding memory is back near its long-term mean, and price-to-book has compressed while ROE remains elevated. These charts do not capture the latest selloff.
JPM expects hyperscaler datacenter capex to rise 85% in 2026 and another 70% in 2027, approaching $1 trillion annually. Aggregate public cloud revenue growth has accelerated to 50% y/y.

AI token demand is growing roughly 17x y/y per JPM, re-accelerating after the August-September slowdown. Compute remains scarce, with short-term contracts priced at $40-50 per watt despite neocloud funding concerns. Falling token prices are not reducing compute demand.

In Q3 the four major cloud providers raised quarterly capex by roughly $45bn versus about $13bn of incremental cloud revenue. The note says this is not a like-for-like return calculation because capex also supports internal workloads. The market is questioning the economics of supplying AI, not demand for it.

JPM says the classic semiconductor cycle-peak warning signs remain largely absent: rising inventories, shortening lead times and collapsing compute prices. Forward net income estimates for Asian tech continue to rise.

Taiwan, the last major AI market standing until last week, has joined the liquidation. The note frames the open question as a positioning-driven washout versus genuine deterioration in AI demand. JPM remains constructive.

sector_views.rationale: JPM remains constructive because earnings revisions are positive, valuations are near historical averages and cycle-peak warning signs are absent. The note acknowledges that price action is challenging this view.

earnings_insights: Roughly 80% of Asian tech companies were still seeing positive earnings revisions when JPM published its report (JPM figure, estimate revisions, not reported results).
Forward net income estimates for Asian tech continue to rise per JPM (estimates, not reported results).
risk_factors: Earnings expectations could start catching down to prices, which the note names as the real danger.
Capex is growing much faster than incremental cloud revenue (about $45bn versus $13bn in Q3), which raises questions about the economics of supplying AI.
charts_described: JPM charts show forward P/E for Asian tech excluding memory near its long-term mean, and price-to-book compressed while ROE remains elevated. The note says they do not capture the latest selloff.
vol_and_positioning: The note describes the selloff as possibly another violent positioning reset, in contrast with a fundamental deterioration in AI demand.
Asian tech has had its fourth 20%+ correction since 2022. Taiwan has now joined the liquidation after being the last major AI market holding up.

tension_points.bull_case: Per JPM, about 80% of companies have positive earnings revisions, forward net income estimates keep rising, valuations are near historical averages, and cycle-peak warning signs (rising inventories, shorter lead times, collapsing compute prices) are absent.
tension_points.bear_case: The selloff has intensified and Taiwan has joined it. Q3 capex rose about $45bn against about $13bn of incremental cloud revenue, and neocloud funding concerns persist. The risk is that earnings expectations start catching down to prices.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Earnings expectations starting to catch down to prices, meaning estimate revisions turn negative.

theme_stances.key_argument: Prices have fallen while earnings revisions stay positive and cycle-peak warning signs are absent.
theme_stances.evidence: The charts are breaking. The earnings cycle, at least so far, isn't.
